title: Phân tích Kỹ thuật: Windows 11 Home vs Pro cho Doanh nghiệp & Lập trình viên
summary:
Phân tích Kỹ thuật: Windows 11 Home vs Pro cho Doanh nghiệp & Lập trình viên

Khi triển khai môi trường làm việc kỹ thuật hoặc trang bị máy tính văn phòng, câu hỏi thường gặp nhất giữa các Tech Lead và Quản trị viên IT là: Nên sử dụng Windows 11 Home hay nâng cấp lên Windows 11 Pro?

Bài viết này đi sâu vào kiến trúc bảo mật tầng phần cứng, ảo hóa cục bộ và tính tuân thủ pháp lý của hai phiên bản này.

1. Bảng So Sánh Kỹ Thuật Chi Tiết

Tính năng cốt lõi Windows 11 Home Windows 11 Pro Ý nghĩa thực tế
Mã hóa BitLocker Không (Chỉ có Device Encryption cơ bản) Có (Full Volume Encryption với chip TPM 2.0) Chống tháo ổ cứng cắm máy khác để đánh cắp dữ liệu mã nguồn
Windows Hyper-V / Sandbox Không hỗ trợ Hỗ trợ Native Khởi chạy máy ảo test code, Docker Desktop chạy mượt mà không cần WSL phụ
Group Policy (GPO) Bị vô hiệu hóa Đầy đủ quyền điều khiển Đẩy chính sách bảo mật mạng nội bộ tập trung cho hàng trăm máy trạm
Bộ nhớ RAM tối đa 128 GB (1 CPU) 2 TB (Lên tới 2 CPU vật lý) Phù hợp cho máy trạm Workstation render 3D và biên dịch Big Data
Remote Desktop (RDP Host) Chỉ làm Client Làm Host & Client Kết nối trực tiếp vào máy tính văn phòng từ xa mà không phụ thuộc phần mềm thứ ba

2. Rủi Ro Tuân Thủ Bản Quyền Doanh Nghiệp (Compliance)

Nhiều doanh nghiệp vừa và nhỏ (SME) lầm tưởng rằng mua laptop cá nhân cài sẵn bản Windows Home là có thể đưa vào công ty sử dụng hợp pháp. Tuy nhiên:

  • Theo điều khoản EULA của Microsoft, các tính năng quản trị miền (Domain Join / Microsoft Entra ID) chỉ khả dụng trên bản Pro trở lên.
  • Khi có các đợt thanh kiểm tra liên ngành về quyền sở hữu trí tuệ phần mềm (Bản quyền tác giả), hóa đơn GTGT ghi rõ phiên bản thương mại hợp lệ là bằng chứng pháp lý duy nhất bảo vệ doanh nghiệp khỏi mức phạt hành chính.

Bạn có thể tham khảo thêm thông tin chi tiết và tài liệu hướng dẫn đối soát tại bản quyền Microsoft chính hãng có hóa đơn VAT.

3. Khuyến Nghị Triển Khai Cho Đội Ngũ Kỹ Thuật

  1. Với Lập trình viên (Developers / DevOps): Bắt buộc sử dụng Windows 11 Pro để kích hoạt tối đa hiệu năng ảo hóa của Docker, WSL2 và cô lập môi trường kiểm thử mã độc bằng Windows Sandbox.
  2. Với Doanh nghiệp có từ 5 nhân sự: Nên tiêu chuẩn hóa ngay từ đầu trên phiên bản Pro để dễ dàng đồng bộ tài khoản Microsoft 365 Business và quản lý dữ liệu tập trung.

title: Why Stateless AI Fails at SRE (And How Contextual Memory Fixes It)
summary:
During a P1 production outage, every minute of downtime costs thousands of dollars. Standard AI assistants lack organizational context, providing generic textbook advice or hallucinating destructive CLI commands.

To solve this, I built NerveCenter, an intelligent SRE agent that replaces generic AI with historically grounded runbooks.

NerveCenter uses Streamlit, Groq (gpt-oss-120b), and Vectorize Hindsight as a dynamic memory layer. When a "Redis OOM Error" alert fires, NerveCenter queries the vector database for similar past incidents. It retrieves Incident 892, outputs the exact redis-cli FLUSHALL ASYNC command used to fix it, and injects the post-mortem notes directly into the context. If flushing the cache previously caused a latency spike, the agent actively warns the engineer before executing the command.

By grounding the LLM in real execution logs, we eliminate hallucinations and prevent repeated mistakes.

Check out the Hindsight GitHub or learn about Vectorize agent memory to see how this works. You can also read the Hindsight docs.

title: Designing the Network Between Clouds: A Planning Outline for Multi-Cloud Estates
summary:
Most multi-cloud architecture diagrams draw each cloud as a tidy box. Inside the boxes there are VPCs, subnets, managed services, and careful labels. Between the boxes there is usually a single line, sometimes labelled just "VPN" or "internet".

That line is where a surprising amount of production pain lives.

As soon as a workload in one cloud genuinely depends on data or services in another — a reporting job reading from a database that stayed behind, an application calling an AI endpoint hosted elsewhere, a failover that suddenly reroutes traffic across providers — the lines between the boxes stop being decoration. They become a network that somebody has to design, secure, document, and debug at 2 a.m.

This is a planning outline for treating inter-cloud connectivity as a designed layer in its own right, before the estate grows enough that retrofitting it becomes expensive.

1. Inventory the flows before choosing any technology

The most common mistake is starting with connection products. Start with flows instead.

For each cross-cloud dependency, write down:

  • Source and destination — which account, VPC/VNet, and region on each side
  • What it carries — application traffic, replication, backups, admin access, inference calls
  • How sensitive it is — does it cross a trust boundary? Does it carry regulated data?
  • What breaks if it stops — a degraded feature, or a full outage?
  • Who owns it — a named team, not "the cloud team" in general

Most estates discover flows nobody remembered creating: a one-off tunnel from a migration two years ago, a peering set up for a demo that quietly became load-bearing. The inventory is unglamorous work, but every later decision — routing, security policy, cost — depends on it being complete.

2. Plan address space and DNS as if there will be a third cloud

Overlapping private address space is the multi-cloud problem that bites earliest and gets discussed least. Two clouds adopted independently often arrive with the same RFC 1918 ranges, because both teams picked 10.0.0.0/16 as the obvious default. The collision only surfaces when a workload in one cloud genuinely needs to reach a service in the other — at which point the fixes are all unpleasant: NAT at the boundary, proxy layers, or renumbering something already running in production.

A few habits prevent most of it:

  • Allocate private ranges centrally, per cloud, per region, per environment — and record the allocations somewhere engineers actually check before creating a new VPC or VNet.
  • Reserve space for future clouds and regions even if there is no current plan for them. Reserving address space costs nothing; renumbering costs weekends.
  • Agree on one DNS resolution convention early. Each cloud resolves names differently, conditional forwarding rules pile up, and an internal service that resolves fine in one environment silently fails in another. Private zones, forwarding rules, and naming conventions should be designed once and applied consistently across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle environments rather than invented per project.

3. Decide deliberately where private paths earn their place

Not every cross-cloud flow needs private connectivity. Public internet routing with TLS and strong authentication is fine for plenty of low-sensitivity, latency-tolerant traffic — and it is simple, cheap, and quick to set up.

Private paths earn their place where one or more of these is true:

  • The traffic carries sensitive or regulated data and the organisation wants it off the public internet entirely.
  • The flow is latency- or jitter-sensitive, such as synchronous replication or real-time inference calls.
  • Predictability matters: internet paths change, and troubleshooting "it was fast yesterday" across two providers and an unknown middle is miserable.
  • An auditor is going to ask, in writing, how traffic between environments is protected — and "the public internet, but encrypted" is not the answer the business wants to give.

Whichever mix an estate ends up with, the decision should be recorded per flow, with the reason. Undocumented exceptions have a way of becoming permanent.

4. Document routing intent, not just the primary path

A link diagram shows the happy path. Operations live on the unhappy ones.

For each important cross-cloud flow, document the intended path for failover as well as for normal operation. Asymmetric routing is a recurring cause of baffling failures: after a failover, return traffic takes a different path than the request, stateful inspection on the new path has no session for it, and packets get dropped in a way that looks — from the application side — like random flakiness.

Writing down "traffic from A to B should return via X, and here is the firewall/NAT behaviour on that path" before the failover happens turns a multi-hour debugging session into a checklist lookup.

5. Treat it as one layer, with one owner

The pattern behind most of the problems above is the same: inter-cloud connections built team by team and project by project, each one reasonable in isolation, adding up to a tangle nobody fully owns or can draw accurately.

The alternative is to treat the network between clouds as its own designed layer — planned address space, consistent DNS, deliberate private paths, documented routing intent, and a single place where those decisions live. That is the layer providers in this space work in: CloudVerg, for example, covers private cloud and multi-cloud networking for US businesses across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle, with platforms such as VergMesh and VergRail for the connectivity side of the estate and zero-trust security and SOC 2 readiness work alongside it: https://cloudverg.com

Whether that layer is built in-house or with outside help, the planning questions are the same.

A short checklist

Before the next cloud, region, or major workload lands:

  • [ ] Every cross-cloud flow inventoried, with an owner and a sensitivity rating
  • [ ] Private address ranges allocated centrally, with space reserved for growth
  • [ ] One DNS naming and resolution convention, applied in every cloud
  • [ ] Per-flow decision on private vs public paths, with the reason recorded
  • [ ] Failover paths documented, including return-path and stateful-inspection behaviour
  • [ ] One team accountable for the inter-cloud layer as a whole

The boxes in the diagram will keep multiplying. The lines between them deserve the same engineering attention as what is inside them — ideally before, not after, the first cross-cloud incident makes the case the hard way.

title: Git Commands Cheat Sheet for Beginners: 20 Commands You Will Use Every Day
summary:
Originally published on CodingCush.

A Git commands cheat sheet is a short list of the commands you use again and again to save versions of your code, see what changed, work on branches and share your work online. You do not need to memorise hundreds of options. Twenty core commands cover almost all daily work: setting up, staging, committing, checking history, branching, merging, syncing with a remote and safely undoing small mistakes. Learn these well, in the order of a normal working day, and Git stops feeling scary and starts feeling like a reliable undo button for your whole project.

First, What Git Is Doing in Simple Words

Git tracks changes in a folder, called a repository. You tell Git which changes to save, Git stores a snapshot called a commit, and each commit remembers the one before it. That chain of snapshots is your project's history. You can return to any earlier snapshot, compare two of them, or let several people build separate lines of history and join them later.

The official site at git-scm.com describes Git as a free and open source distributed version control system designed to handle everything from small to very large projects with speed and efficiency. Distributed means every developer holds a full copy of the history, so most work happens offline, on your own machine, at full speed.

Set Up Once: config and init or clone 

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git init
git clone https://github.com/user/project.git

git config stamps your name and email on your commits; do it once on each new computer. git init turns the current folder into a new repository. git clone downloads an existing project, including its full history, from a site like GitHub. Starting a project yourself means init; joining an existing one means clone. If Git is not installed yet, follow our guide to installing Git on Windows, Mac and Linux first, then come back to this sheet.

The Daily Loop: status, add, commit, diff 

git status
git add index.html
git add .
git commit -m "Add contact form"
git diff
git diff --staged

git status is the command you will type most. It tells you which files changed, which are staged and which branch you are on. Run it whenever you feel lost; it is Git's friendly dashboard. git add moves changes into the staging area, the waiting room for your next commit. Adding one file is precise; git add . stages everything, which is handy but deserves a quick status check first, so a stray file does not hitchhike into history.

git commit -m saves the staged snapshot with a short message. Write messages in plain words about why or what, like "Fix login button on mobile", not "stuff" or "final final v2". Future you, reading history at midnight, says thank you. git diff shows changes you have not staged yet, line by line, and git diff --staged shows exactly what is about to enter the next commit. Checking the diff before committing is the habit that prevents most embarrassing commits.

The official Git website, git-scm.com, describing Git as a free and open source distributed version control system for projects of every size.

See History: log and show 

git log
git log --oneline
git show HEAD
git show a1b2c3d

git log lists commits newest first, with author, date and message. The --oneline form squeezes each commit to one short line, perfect for a quick overview. git show opens one commit and displays exactly what it changed; HEAD means the latest commit, or you can paste a commit's short code from the log. History is not decoration. It answers the two questions developers ask weekly: when did this change, and what exactly changed with it?

Branches: branch, switch, merge 

git branch
git branch new-login-page
git switch new-login-page
git switch -c new-login-page
git merge new-login-page

A branch is a movable label pointing at a commit: a safe line of work where you can experiment without touching the main line. git branch lists branches, creating one does not move you onto it, and git switch moves you there. The -c form creates and switches in one step, which is why you will see it everywhere. When the work is ready, switch back to main and git merge to bring that branch's commits in. Our full guide to Git branches explained walks through creating, switching, merging and deleting branches with pictures in words, so read it after this sheet.

Share and Sync: remote, push, pull, fetch 

git remote -v
git push origin main
git pull
git fetch

A remote is a named address for another copy of the repository, usually on GitHub, and origin is the standard name for your main one. git push uploads your commits; git pull downloads new commits and merges them into your current branch. git fetch is pull's cautious cousin: it downloads without merging, so you can inspect first and merge when ready. The official Git reference documentation explains every command and option, and it is the right place to check an option before trusting a random comment online.

Job Command Remember it as
See what is happening git status The dashboard
Stage changes git add . Pack the box
Save a snapshot git commit -m "message" Seal and label the box
Upload work git push Send the boxes
Download and merge git pull Receive and unpack
Undo a file change git restore file Put it back

Undo Safely: restore and the Gentle Fixes 

git restore index.html
git restore --staged index.html
git commit --amend -m "Better message"

git restore throws away uncommitted changes in one file, so use it only when you are sure that work is unwanted; there is no dustbin to recover it from. With --staged it simply unstages a file while keeping your edits. git commit --amend rewrites your latest commit, handy for fixing a typo in its message or adding a forgotten file, but only before you push it. Shared history is a promise to your team; rewriting your own unpushed history is housekeeping.

A Normal Working Day, Using Only This Sheet

Watch how the twenty commands join into one calm routine. You start with git pull to collect your team's latest work, then git switch -c to open a branch for today's task. While building, you run git status and git diff like glancing in a mirror, git add the finished pieces, and git commit them in small, honest steps. A typo in the last message gets a quick --amend. Before lunch you peek at git log --oneline and feel oddly proud of the tidy story forming. At the end, you switch back to main, git merge your branch, and git push. Nothing heroic happened, and that is exactly the point: good Git work is boring, regular and safe, like saving a document every few minutes instead of once at midnight.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the most used Git command?

For most developers it is git status, followed by add, commit, push and pull. Status is the safe first step whenever you return to a project or feel unsure what state your files are in.

What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?

First, What Git Is Doing in Simple Words

title: Putting AI Agents on Call: How We Built an Autonomous SRE War Room in Slack with Switch and Wispr Flow
summary:
Putting AI Agents on Call: How We Built an Autonomous SRE War Room in Slack with Switch and Wispr Flow

A deep-dive tutorial and architectural walkthrough for the Flip the Switch Hackathon (WeMakeDevs × DevTools Academy × Switch).

The 2:00 AM Problem: Why Solitary Coding Copilots Fail During Incidents

Every software engineer knows the sinking feeling of a critical production outage in the middle of the night.

PagerDuty sounds its alarm. Error rate graphs spike into the red on Datadog. Customer tickets flood Zendesk. In Slack, engineers scramble into a chaotic #incident-emergency channel, exchanging frantic questions:

"Which commit went out in the 09:40 UTC deploy?"

"Is cart-service throwing 500s because of the database migration or the coupon parser?"

"Can someone write a quick script to test the failure locally?"

"Who has permissions to execute a rollback to v2.13.2?"

Over the past two years, AI coding assistants like Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Codex, and Cursor have revolutionized how we write software. But notice where they live: isolated in a single developer's IDE or terminal.

When a multi-million-dollar production system breaks down, your company doesn't need an isolated assistant typing silently in someone’s local editor. Your company needs an active teammate in the incident room.

In this deep dive, we walk through how we built OpsSwitch—an autonomous SRE incident response squad running inside Slack and Discord. Powered by Switch, OpsSwitch intercepts outage alerts, pinpoints offending commits, executes local reproduction scripts, and prepares safe rollbacks with human-in-the-loop sign-off—all orchestrated hands-free using Wispr Flow voice dictation.

1. Meet Switch: Open Source Infrastructure for AI Teammates

Before building, we asked: Can't we just write a simple Slack webhook bot hooked up to an LLM API?

The answer is an emphatic no. A simple webhook bot suffers from three fatal architectural flaws:

  1. No Shared Chronology: A traditional bot is stateless; it cannot observe the evolving shared context between multiple engineers and peer agents over hours of troubleshooting.
  2. Alert Fatigue & Channel Pollution: Dumping hundreds of raw stack trace lines, terminal logs, and git diffs into a public Slack channel drowns out human coordination.
  3. Severe Credential Risk: Injecting GitHub tokens, AWS keys, or Datadog credentials directly into an LLM's system prompt creates catastrophic prompt-injection vulnerabilities.

This is where Switch changes the paradigm. Switch is open-source infrastructure designed to bring AI agents directly into team chat (Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord, Telegram, and Mattermost).

   Human Engineers (Slack / Discord) ──┐
                                       ├─► [Switch Room] ◄─► [Agent Host] ◄─► [LLM Harness]
   AI Teammates (Claude / Codex / SRE) ──┘   (Shared Log)      (Secure Broker)  (Claude / OpenAI)

In Switch:

  • Every channel is a room: Agents show up with their own distinct avatar, name, system prompt, and capabilities.
  • Rooms can be linked: Context flows cleanly across channels through bi-directional links (intake ↔ war-room), preventing public channel noise.
  • Zero-leakage credential broker: Agents never touch raw API tokens. Tools (GitHub, Sentry, Datadog) are executed over loopback MCP proxies where Switch's session host applies credentials securely.
  • Language-agnostic protocol: Any agent speaking the Agent Protocol (Server-Sent Events in, HTTP out) can collaborate in the room.

2. System Architecture: The Multi-Room Incident Squad

OpsSwitch structures the incident lifecycle across two linked rooms and three specialized AI teammates:

graph LR
    subgraph Intake_Channel ["#sre-incident-intake (Public)"]
        Alert["Incoming Webhook / Human Alert"]
        TriagerIntake["ops-triager"]
        UserLead["On-Call Lead (@Farhan)"]
    end

    subgraph WarRoom_Channel ["#sre-incident-war-room (Private)"]
        TriagerWar["ops-triager"]
        Investigator["ops-investigator"]
        Remediator["ops-remediator"]
    end

    Alert --> TriagerIntake
    TriagerIntake -->|SEV-1 Escalation| TriagerWar
    TriagerWar -->|Hands off error context| Investigator
    Investigator -->|Diffs git + runs repro script| Remediator
    Remediator -->|Awaits Sign-Off Card| UserLead
    UserLead -->|"Approved. Roll it back."| Remediator

The Three AI Teammates:

1. ops-triager (Intake & Classification)

Listens in #sre-incident-intake. Analyzes symptoms and error rates, categorizes severity from SEV-1 (Catastrophic revenue outage) to SEV-4 (Minor cosmetic discrepancy), and escalates high-severity incidents into the private #sre-incident-war-room.

2. ops-investigator (Telemetry & Root-Cause Diagnosis)

Sits in #sre-incident-war-room. Upon escalation, it queries the Switch GitHub and Sentry connectors, analyzes recent commits across the deployment window, identifies the suspected commit, and generates a minimal 4-line reproduction script (repro.py) inside its local sandbox. It runs the repro script and reports verified traceback output.

3. ops-remediator (Mitigation & Governance Gatekeeper)

Formulates the rollback PR or patch branch. Posts an interactive Authorization Card in the war room and enforces a strict human gate: it refuses to touch production without explicit confirmation from an authenticated human on-call lead. Once approved, it merges the PR, polls healthcheck endpoints back to 200 OK, and posts a full post-mortem to the intake room.

3. Step-by-Step Setup: Zero to Running in 15 Minutes

Here is how you can deploy OpsSwitch yourself:

Step 1: Install Switch Console & Dependencies

Clone the Switch repository and start the supporting services:

# 1. Clone repository
git clone https://github.com/sandbox-quantum/switch.git
cd switch

# 2. Initialize secrets and start PostgreSQL & Mattermost in Docker
just init-env
uv sync --project core
just up
just migrate

# 3. Launch Switch Core backend (http://localhost:8000)
just run

Download and launch the Switch Console desktop application for your platform (GitHub Releases). Point it at your local server (http://localhost:8000).

Step 2: Define the Switch Template

In Switch Console, click Templates → Import Custom Template and load the OpsSwitch specification:

version: 1

params:
  team:
    type: string
    default: "sre"
  provider:
    type: provider
    default: [claude, codex, opencode]
  bridge:
    type: bridge
    default: [$first]

agents:
  - name: "{team}-triager"
    description: "Ingests alerts, classifies severity, and escalates to war room"
    addressing: anyone
    provider: "{provider}"
    instructions: |
      You are the incident triager for {team}.
      Monitor {team}-incident-intake. Classify alerts (SEV-1 to SEV-4).
      Escalate SEV-1 and SEV-2 incidents into {team}-incident-war-room tagged to @{team}-investigator.

  - name: "{team}-investigator"
    description: "SRE diagnostic specialist"
    addressing: owner-agents
    provider: "{provider}"
    instructions: |
      You are the SRE investigator in {team}-incident-war-room.
      Inspect recent git commits and error traces.
      Write and run the smallest reproduction script that confirms the bug.
      Tag @{team}-remediator with verified output.

  - name: "{team}-remediator"
    description: "Remediation and rollback specialist"
    addressing: owner-agents
    provider: "{provider}"
    instructions: |
      You are the remediation engineer in {team}-incident-war-room.
      Prepare rollback PRs or emergency patches.
      STRICT RULE: Never execute production changes without explicit sign-off from @{$creator}.

group:
  name: "{team} Incident Command"
  description: "Autonomous multi-room SRE incident squad"

rooms:
  - name: "{team}-incident-intake"
    bridge: "{bridge}"
    agents: ["{team}-triager"]
    users: ["{$creator}"]
  - name: "{team}-incident-war-room"
    bridge: "{bridge}"
    agents: ["{team}-triager", "{team}-investigator", "{team}-remediator"]
    users: ["{$creator}"]

links:
  - from: "{team}-incident-intake"
    to: "{team}-incident-war-room"
    label: escalations

Click Launch Group. Switch automatically creates the linked Slack channels and spins up the agents in isolated local working directories!

4. Building by Voice: The Wispr Flow Experience

One of the most transformative elements of this build was participating in the Code with Wispr track. Rather than typing out thousands of lines of prompt instructions, architectural schemas, and documentation by hand, we used Wispr Flow Pro to dictate everything.

       [Spoken Voice Stream] 
                 │
                 ▼
          [Wispr Flow AI]
                 │
                 ├─► Transcribes natural conversational speech
                 ├─► Formats Markdown, indentation & YAML
                 ▼
          [Switch Agent System Prompts & Instructions]

Why Dictation Accelerates Agent Development:

  1. Natural Conversational Nuance: When you write system prompts for AI agents, you are describing human behavior ("If an alert looks like a payment failure, immediately restate it in one line and ping the war room"). Speaking naturally produces far richer, more nuanced agent instructions than terse typed bullet points.
  2. Frictionless Context Capture: During live debugging, we dictated the reproduction script requirements directly into the terminal, allowing us to maintain flow state without wrist strain.
  3. Scorecard Verification: By the end of our build, Wispr Flow's Insights dashboard logged over 6,500 words dictated across our planning and agent instructions, cutting our development cycle by nearly 40%.

5. Simulating a Live SEV-1 Outage: The 8-Minute Resolution

To test OpsSwitch under realistic conditions, we created an intentional failure in a mock microservice (cart-service) where an unhandled NullPointerException occurs whenever an empty coupon code is passed at checkout.

Here is what unfolded in Slack:

T + 00:30 (Intake Channel)

Farhan (On-Call Lead):

"@sre-triager checkout service is throwing HTTP 500 errors since the 09:40 UTC deploy. Users cannot complete purchases."

@sre-triager:

"🚨 Acknowledged. Revenue impact detected on /checkout. Classified as **SEV-1. Escalating incident to #sre-incident-war-room."

T + 01:15 (War Room Channel)

@sre-triager:

"Escalation from intake: Checkout 500s reported at 09:40 UTC. @sre-investigator please initiate diagnostic audit."

@sre-investigator:

"Examining deployment commits. Inspecting git commit f3c8a91 ('feat: coupon code parser') merged at 09:38 UTC.

Generating minimal reproduction script test_repro.py in local sandbox..."

# test_repro.py generated by ops-investigator
import requests
response = requests.post("http://localhost:5000/checkout", json={"cart_id": 102, "coupon": None})
print(f"Status: {response.status_code}, Body: {response.text}")

@sre-investigator:

"Reproduction confirmed: Exit code 1. java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke String.trim() because coupon is null at line 142. Tagging @sre-remediator to prepare rollback."

T + 03:00 (Human Sign-Off Gate)

@sre-remediator:

"⚠️ **AUTHORIZATION REQUIRED: Prepared Rollback PR #412 (Revert commit f3c8a91 to restore stable v2.13.2).

**Risk Level:* Low (No database migrations affected).

@farhan please reply 'Approved. Roll it back.' to execute."*

Farhan (On-Call Lead):

"Approved. Roll it back."

T + 04:30 (Execution & Verification)

@sre-remediator:

"Approval verified. Merged PR #412 to main. Triggered automated deployment.

Polling healthcheck endpoint /healthz...

[200 OK] Verified. System error rate returned to 0.00%. Incident resolved. Handing off to @sre-triager."

T + 05:00 (Executive Post-Mortem in Intake)

@sre-triager:

"✅ **INCIDENT RESOLVED: Checkout service restored to 100% health.

**Root Cause:* NPE in commit f3c8a91 handling null coupon codes.

Remediation: Reverted via PR #412.

Total Time to Restore (TTR): 8 minutes."*

6. Key Learnings & Takeaways

Building OpsSwitch taught us several crucial lessons about the future of multi-agent engineering:

  1. Topology Matters More Than Model Size: Trying to force a single massive LLM prompt to handle triage, investigation, and git operations resulted in hallucinations and channel noise. Giving three smaller, focused agents their own rooms and explicit responsibilities produced near-deterministic reliability.
  2. Human Governance Is Non-Negotiable: Autonomous agents should do the heavy lifting of gathering evidence and staging solutions, but production write access must always be guarded by authenticated human intent.
  3. Open Standards Win: Switch's clean Server-Sent Events architecture made integrating our custom python diagnostics effortless. Because Switch doesn't lock you into a proprietary platform, our incident room can run self-hosted on our own Kubernetes clusters with total data sovereignty.

Try It Yourself!

    • OpsSwitch Flagship Showcase: https://github.com/farhanmallik05/OpsSwitch
    • Switch Core Contributions Fork: https://github.com/farhanmallik05/switch

title: 0 9 * * 1-5 is weekdays at 09:00
summary:
A morning job was saved as 0 9 * * 1-5. On Vixie cron and cronie that is 09:00 Monday through Friday. Monday is 1 and Friday is 5, so the range 1-5 is those five days. The day-of-month field is a star, which means every day of the month, so the weekday field is the only limit on the day. The either-day rule starts only when both day fields are restricted. The four lines below are that same five-field form.

0 * * * *       # every hour, at minute 0
0 0 * * *       # every day at 00:00
0 9 * * *       # every day at 09:00
0 9 * * 1-5     # Monday through Friday at 09:00

What each line fires

0 * * * * fires 24 times a day, at the top of each hour. 0 0 * * * fires once, at midnight. 0 9 * * * is every day at 09:00, Saturday and Sunday included. 0 9 * * 1-5 keeps that minute and that hour, and leaves Saturday and Sunday out.

09:00 is the daemon's clock. The fields are read in that timezone, so the hour is not necessarily UTC. Vixie cron documents a CRON_TZ setting for one crontab. Whether the package on the host honors it is a question for that host's crontab(5).

Sunday, and the sentence the generator writes

On Vixie cron and cronie, Sunday is 0 and also 7. Some other schedulers accept only 0 for Sunday. Read crontab(5) on the host before you use 7. The cron expression generator writes numbers. For 0 9 * * 1-5 its sentence is "at minute 0, at hour 9, on weekday 1-5". It does not spell out Monday through Friday, and it does not install the job.

0 9 * * 5 is a different line. The generator reads that single 5 as Friday: "at minute 0, at hour 9, on Friday". The range 1-5 is the five weekdays. A lone 5 is Friday only.

One tip

A day field that starts with *, including */2, is unrestricted. The page for a line such as 0 9 1 * 5, where both day fields are restricted, is https://kepttools.com/guides/cron-both-day-fields

The field table and the rest of the questions are in the guide: https://kepttools.com/guides/cron-every-5-minutes

title: Kubernetes: limpiar datos de email en CI sin perder señales
summary:
Un pipeline de CI puede terminar en verde y dejar un problema invisible: buzones de prueba, secretos temporales y mensajes de verificación que siguen existiendo mucho después de que acaba el job.

En equipos que ejecutan pruebas de registro, OAuth o recuperación de contraseña dentro de Kubernetes, el fallo suele aparecer días después. El clúster parece sano, pero los datos de email se acumulan, los artefactos pierden contexto y nadie sabe qué ejecución creó cada recurso.

La solución no es borrar todo al final sin mirar. Es dar a cada ejecución una identidad, separar la evidencia mínima de los datos sensibles y hacer la limpieza idempotente.

El síntoma: el pipeline termina, pero el buzón queda vivo

Imaginemos un job que crea un namespace efímero, levanta la aplicación y solicita un generador de cuentas de correo temporal para validar un enlace de activación. La prueba pasa. El runner se cierra. Sin embargo, pueden quedar tres cosas:

  • Un buzón asociado a la ejecución.
  • Un secreto de Kubernetes con una dirección o token de acceso.
  • Un log que dice “email recibido”, pero no indica qué mensaje ni qué versión lo generó.

Cuando llega un fallo intermitente, el equipo reintenta y crea otro conjunto de recursos. Despues de varias horas, la limpieza manual se convierte en parte del incidente.

Qué debe identificar cada ejecución

El primer cambio es usar un run_id que viaje por todo el flujo. No debe depender solo del nombre del branch, porque dos ejecuciones del mismo branch pueden ocurrir al mismo tiempo.

Un identificador útil aparece en:

  1. La etiqueta del namespace o del recurso temporal.
  2. El asunto o encabezado técnico del mensaje de prueba.
  3. El nombre del artefacto de CI.
  4. Los logs de la aplicación y del consumidor.

Por ejemplo:

metadata:
  labels:
    ci.run_id: "run-20261107-0522-a81f"
    ci.owner: "checkout-tests"
    data.class: "synthetic-email"

La etiqueta data.class ayuda a distinguir datos sintéticos de cualquier dato que no debe tocar un proceso automático. Parece pequeño, pero hace la limpieza mucho mas segura.

Separar evidencia de datos temporales

Un error común es guardar el contenido completo del email como artefacto porque “puede servir para depurar”. En realidad, el HTML suele contener tokens, nombres y enlaces que ya no hacen falta cuando la prueba termina.

Conviene conservar una evidencia compacta, por ejemplo:

{
  "run_id": "run-20261107-0522-a81f",
  "message_id": "msg-7b2c",
  "event": "verification_received",
  "latency_ms": 1840,
  "result": "passed"
}

El cuerpo del mensaje puede eliminarse o redacted en el origen, según la capacidad del sistema de email. Para diagnosticar una demora, message_id, estado y latencia suelen ser mas útiles que guardar todo el contenido.

También ayuda registrar el momento de expiración. Si el buzón debe vivir diez minutos, esa regla debe estar en los metadatos y no solo en la memoria del desarrollador. Un expires_at explícito permite que un reconciliador actúe aunque el runner se corte.

Un patrón sencillo para Kubernetes

Hay dos caminos razonables, y pueden convivir:

Limpieza al terminar el job. El pipeline intenta borrar el namespace, el secreto y el buzón. Es rapido y barato, pero no cubre un runner cancelado, un timeout o un nodo perdido.

Reconciliación periódica. Un proceso busca recursos con data.class=synthetic-email, compara expires_at con la hora actual y elimina los vencidos. Es la red de seguridad que evita depender de un único finally.

El reconciliador debe ser conservador. Primero comprueba que el recurso pertenece al entorno de pruebas, luego confirma que está vencido y finalmente elimina por run_id. Si una ejecución todavía está activa, no debe asumir que su buzón está huérfano solo por ser antiguo.

Para mantener la operación trazable, cada decisión puede producir un evento pequeño: kept, expired, deleted o skipped_active. Esos eventos son mas faciles de buscar que un log narrativo largo. Para trabajos programados, un contrato de salida con estado, motivo y run_id también evita que un agente o un job aguas abajo interprete un borrado incompleto como éxito; este contrato de salida para el job es un buen patrón aplicable.

Limpieza segura y observable

Antes de activar el borrado automático, haría estas comprobaciones:

  • Modo de observación: durante un día, el reconciliador solo informa qué eliminaría.
  • Permiso limitado: la cuenta de servicio solo puede leer y borrar recursos con las etiquetas esperadas.
  • Idempotencia: borrar un buzón ya eliminado debe producir un estado conocido, no una alerta falsa.
  • Retención de evidencia: conserva el resumen de la ejecución por un periodo corto y definido.
  • Métrica de residuos: mide recursos vencidos, edad máxima y tiempo de limpieza.
  • Alerta útil: avisa cuando el volumen o la edad superan un umbral, no por cada recurso individual.

La telemetria debe responder tres preguntas: qué ejecución creó el dato, por que todavía existe y qué acción tomó el sistema. Si no puede responderlas, hay automatización, pero no hay control operacional.

Un caso especialmente delicado es el fallo parcial. La prueba puede pasar, pero la limpieza del buzón fallar. El resultado del job debería separar test_status de cleanup_status; de ese modo, el equipo sabe que la funcionalidad está bien y que queda una tarea de higiene pendiente.

Checklist para SRE

Antes de considerar terminado el diseño, revisa:

  • ¿Cada recurso de email tiene run_id, propietario y expiración?
  • ¿La evidencia excluye tokens y cuerpos innecesarios?
  • ¿Existe un reconciliador para jobs cancelados o nodos perdidos?
  • ¿El borrado está restringido a datos sintéticos?
  • ¿Se puede explicar cada decisión en los logs?
  • ¿Hay una métrica de recursos vencidos y otra de tiempo de limpieza?
  • ¿El proceso esta probado con ejecuciones simultáneas?

No hace falta empezar con un operador complejo. Un job pequeño, etiquetas consistentes y una política clara ya reducen mucho el riesgo. Incluso una búsqueda rápida de “tem email” en documentación interna debería llevar a la misma definición de datos sintéticos, no a una colección de scripts distintos.

Preguntas frecuentes

¿Debo borrar el mensaje antes de guardar evidencia?

Guarda primero un resumen sin secretos y elimina el cuerpo tan pronto como termine la aserción necesaria. Si una investigación necesita más detalle, usa una retención explícita y con acceso limitado.

¿Qué pasa si el pipeline se cancela?

El reconciliador debe detectar el expires_at vencido. No dependas únicamente de un paso final del runner, porque ese paso no siempre se ejecuta.

¿Cuándo conviene usar un namespace por ejecución?

Cuando las pruebas cambian configuración o despliegan varios componentes. Para una prueba pequeña puede bastar con etiquetas y nombres únicos, siempre que la limpieza pueda aislar exactamente sus recursos.

La idea central es simple: los datos de email de CI son recursos operativos, no basura anónima. Si tienen identidad, expiración y evidencia mínima, Kubernetes puede ayudar a limpiarlos sin borrar las señales que un equipo SRE necesita para entender el siguiente incidente.

title: The Beget Cyberattack Data Loss: Why Half of Customers Won't Get a Backup
summary:
The Beget Cyberattack Data Loss: Why Half of Customers Won't Get a Backup

The Beget cyberattack data loss is the story of a Russian hosting provider that lost all data in its VPS, S3, and Kubernetes cloud infrastructure after attackers compromised its management plane overnight on November 1-2, 2026. By a November 6 update, the news had gotten worse: according to comss.ru's reporting, Beget now says file-level VPS backups, the one category it had initially said survived, will only be recoverable for about half of affected customers.

Jump to the estimate that got worse, not better if you want that detail first.

What Attackers Actually Did

Tadviser's incident record states plainly that "attackers gained access to the system managing the entire architecture and executed scripts that wiped the data." This is a management-plane compromise, not a ransomware encryption event or a data-exfiltration breach. The attacker's goal, as far as Beget's own disclosures describe it, was destruction: once inside the control system that manages Beget's infrastructure, the intrusion deleted data rather than encrypting it for ransom or quietly copying it out.

The destruction was total within the cloud segment specifically. All data in VPS, S3, and Kubernetes was lost, according to Beget's own Telegram announcement as translated and reported by iz.ru, along with CDN configuration and IP address settings. Binary VPS backups, full disk images that would have let customers restore a server to its exact prior state, were destroyed completely. Beget said at the time that file-level backups, individual files rather than whole-disk images, had survived.

The Estimate That Got Worse, Not Better

That survival claim didn't hold up as cleanly as first reported, however. Beget's November 6 update, per comss.ru, revised the file-backup recovery estimate downward: "по актуальной оценке компании, файловые резервные копии будут доступны только половине пользователей," meaning the company's current assessment is that file backups will be available to only half of users, not the near-complete recovery implied by its earlier messaging.

Even where a backup copy does exist, comss.ru reports that each one has to be manually matched to its specific customer and all of that customer's associated data, a process the company describes as time-consuming rather than automated. For some clients, Beget's own internal records linking an account to its services were also lost, meaning those associations can't simply be restored; they have to be reconstructed from scratch.

What's Actually Recovering, and What's a Harder Rebuild

The recovery picture Beget has published is uneven by design, not by accident, and the unevenness tracks directly to how centralized each affected system was. Dedicated servers that customers administer themselves were restored quickly, within roughly a day, because Beget's own infrastructure compromise never touched systems the customer, not Beget, controls. DNS management for domains in the .ru, .рф, and .su zones came back next. Virtual hosting, ordinary websites rather than VPS instances, was reported by comss.ru as more than 60% restored by November 5-6, with the remainder dependent on backup restoration rather than a simple server restart.

Social-media monitoring firm Dark Web Intelligence's recovery update, citing Beget's own November 5 status report, lists 60% of shared-hosting servers back online (up from 35% the day before), 40% of managed dedicated servers restored, and billing paused entirely while the affected categories of service remain unrestored. The same post adds an important qualifier: "figures and timelines are Beget's own estimates, not guarantees," and notes that ransomware has not been established as the mechanism, consistent with Beget's own description of deletion scripts following management-plane access rather than an encryption payload.

VPS, S3, and Kubernetes remain the hardest case, because those are precisely the systems where the deleted binary backups would have mattered most, and where the newly revised 50% file-backup recovery rate leaves the other half of affected customers dependent entirely on whatever backups they kept outside Beget's own infrastructure.

title: The OpenSSH sshole Vulnerability: Two Different Kinds of 'No Match' Accidentally Matched
summary:
The OpenSSH sshole Vulnerability: Two Different Kinds of 'No Match' Accidentally Matched

The OpenSSH sshole vulnerability, CVE-2026-123158, let a remote attacker log into an account with no password set on Alpine Linux, using nothing but an unusually long password string. According to The Hacker News, threat intelligence firm Previdian observed the first exploitation attempt less than nine hours after the CVE was published, and confirmed successful root access on a honeypot running real Alpine Linux and OpenSSH.

Jump to why this took forty years to notice for the part of this story that's genuinely remarkable.

What the Bug Actually Does

The mechanism, as documented in detail by ox.security's technical analysis, comes down to two unrelated systems independently choosing the same sentinel character to mean "this will never match," then being compared against each other. An account with no password set stores a single asterisk, *, in its password field. Separately, musl's crypt() function, the cryptographic hashing function Alpine Linux's standard library uses, returns that same asterisk when it rejects a password as too long, specifically anything between 257 and 1,024 bytes, a limit musl added in 2012 specifically to prevent denial-of-service attacks from oversized inputs.

When OpenSSH's sshd runs without PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules), which is how Alpine's default openssh-server package is built, it hashes the submitted password itself and compares the result directly against the stored field. Submit a password long enough to trip musl's length limit, and crypt() returns *. Compare that against a stored field of *, and the strings match. SocRadar's writeup confirms the authentication succeeds on that comparison alone, no actual password required.

Why This Took Forty Years to Notice

The sentinel-collision framing isn't editorializing, it's how the researcher who found the bug, Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield, traces the problem. Sploitus's technical timeline lays out the chain explicitly: Unix adopted * to mean "no password" as far back as 1980's 3BSD documentation. musl, independently, started returning * for a failed crypt() call in 2012, and added the 256-byte length cap, the actual trigger condition, seventeen days later in the same month.

OpenSSH added salt-borrowing logic in 2016 to fix a username-enumeration bug, CVE-2016-6210, which is the piece that lets sshd reach for a real password hash elsewhere on the system to generate a comparison salt in the first place. None of these three changes, made across a span of decades by different maintainers for different reasons, was wrong on its own. The vulnerability only exists where all three intersect.

That's also why reproducing it required brute force rather than code review. ox.security's research describes building sshd in every combination of glibc, musl, PAM, and no-PAM, then firing roughly 17,600 deliberately unusual login attempts at each build. Every combination behaved correctly except exactly one: musl without PAM.

Who Is Actually Exposed

The exposure conditions are narrow but common in one specific context. According to BigGo's reporting, four conditions must all hold simultaneously: the SSH daemon must be built without PAM, password authentication must be enabled (OpenSSH's own default), at least one account must have * in its password field, and at least one other local account must carry a real $5$ or $6$ hash for sshd to borrow a salt from.

Alpine Linux's default openssh-server package satisfies the first condition out of the box. Help Net Security's reporting quotes the researcher listing OpenWrt, Buildroot, and Yocto as other musl-based systems worth checking, "along with a lot of the docker images you've pulled." Debian, Ubuntu, RHEL, and anything else built on glibc are confirmed unaffected; OpenSSH maintainer Damien Miller stated explicitly that glibc-based systems and PAM-authenticated setups fall outside the bug's scope.

What This Means If You Run Alpine-Based Containers or VMs

Our verdict: patch immediately if you're exposed, but recognize that exposure here depends on a narrow, specific configuration, not on simply running Alpine. The honeypot compromise happened in under nine hours, so the window for "patch when convenient" has already closed for anyone reachable on the public internet.

  • Upgrade to OpenSSH 10.6p2 or your distribution's patched package, which Alpine has backported all the way to version 3.16 according to SocRadar's version table, then restart sshd. Upgrading the package alone does not restart a running daemon.
  • If you can't patch immediately, set PasswordAuthentication no and restart sshd. This was independently verified as an effective mitigation by multiple researchers, and it has the side benefit of closing off password-guessing attacks generally, not just this specific bug.
  • Audit for accounts with * in /etc/shadow on any musl-based host, especially cloud-init images where a default "alpine" user with passwordless doas to root is documented as present in official tiny-cloud images. That combination, a passwordless admin account plus any other account with a real password hash, is the exact precondition this bug needs.

FAQ

What is the OpenSSH sshole vulnerability, CVE-2026-123158?

It's a password authentication bypass affecting OpenSSH on Linux systems that use the musl C library without PAM, most notably Alpine Linux's default configuration. An attacker can submit a password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long to an account that has no password set, and musl's crypt() function returns an error value that happens to match the stored "no password" marker, causing sshd to accept the login.

Has CVE-2026-123158 been exploited in the wild?

Yes. According to Previdian's telemetry, as reported by The Hacker News, the first exploitation attempt occurred less than nine hours after the CVE was published, and the firm confirmed successful root access on a honeypot running Alpine Linux and OpenSSH. Telemetry showed a total of eight exploitation attempts from a single IP address.

Does this vulnerability affect Debian, Ubuntu, or Red Hat systems?

No. The bug requires musl libc, which Alpine Linux and a handful of embedded/lightweight distributions use. Standard Ubuntu, Debian, and Red Hat systems are built on glibc and are confirmed unaffected, as is any system where sshd authenticates through PAM instead of its internal password-checking path.

What We Checked Before Publishing

We cross-referenced the vulnerability mechanism across ox.security's and Sploitus's independent technical breakdowns, confirmed the exploitation timeline through The Hacker News' and Help Net Security's reporting of Previdian's telemetry, and verified the affected-versions table against SocRadar's published list of patched Alpine packages. We did not find any outlet confirming exploitation volume beyond Previdian's eight recorded attempts from one IP address, and we've reported that specific, limited figure rather than implying broader in-the-wild activity.

I'm Rohit, founder of Krova Cloud: every Cube ships with key-based SSH access configured from first boot, not password authentication left on by default. That's not a defense against this specific musl-and-no-PAM intersection, our control plane isn't built that way, but it's the same underlying principle this bug illustrates: a default that's convenient in isolation can become a liability the moment it combines with some other default nobody thought to check against it. title: Your CPU Quota Is a Budget, Not a Percentage: Practical cgroup v2 CPU Control on Linux
summary:
A batch job gets CPUQuota=50%. The box still goes to 100% CPU, the API on the same host starts missing deadlines, and someone "fixes" it by raising the quota to 200%. Now the batch job is eating two full cores and the API is still slow.

The number felt like a percentage of the machine. The kernel treats it as microseconds of CPU time per period. Those are the same thing only if you know the period, how many threads are runnable, and what happens when the budget runs out. That last part is what usually surprises people: a cgroup that exceeds its quota is not slowed down proportionally. It is stopped until the next period starts.

cgroup v2's CPU controller has three separate mechanisms that answer three different questions. Mixing them up is why CPU limits feel unpredictable.

Three questions, three knobs

What you actually want systemd setting Kernel interface
"This unit must never exceed X CPU" CPUQuota= cpu.max
"Under contention, this unit should win" CPUWeight= cpu.weight
"This unit may only run on these cores" AllowedCPUs= cpuset.cpus
"Only use CPU nobody else wants" CPUWeight=idle cpu.idle

They compose, but they are not interchangeable. A quota is enforced by throttling. A weight is enforced by the scheduler's fairness math and does exactly nothing when the machine is idle. A cpuset changes placement, not capacity.

The arithmetic of cpu.max

The file is two numbers:

$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/ffmpeg-worker.service/cpu.max
200000 100000

The format is $MAX $PERIOD, both in microseconds. This group may consume up to 200 ms of CPU time in every 100 ms period, which is two CPUs' worth. The default is max 100000: unlimited quota, 100 ms period. Writing a single number updates only $MAX; writing max removes the limit.

So the conversion is:

CPUs = MAX / PERIOD
cpu.max Meaning
max 100000 Unlimited
100000 100000 1 CPU
25000 100000 25% of one CPU
200000 100000 2 CPUs
50000 50000 1 CPU, shorter 50 ms period

systemd's CPUQuota= is a percentage of one CPU, which is why the man page tells you to use values above 100% for more than one CPU. CPUQuota=150% becomes 150000 100000. CPUQuotaPeriodSec= changes the second field; it defaults to 100 ms and is clamped to the range the kernel supports, 1 ms to 1000 ms.

The kernel's own floor is 1 ms for quota or period, and the period cannot exceed 1 s. Those limits come from Documentation/scheduler/sched-bwc.rst.

Why a quota feels like stuttering, not slowing

CFS bandwidth control does not ration CPU smoothly. Within a period, the group's quota is handed out to per-CPU run queues in slices as threads become runnable. When the budget is gone, every thread in the group is throttled until the next period refills it.

Picture CPUQuota=25% on a machine with free cores. The group gets 25 ms of runtime per 100 ms. A single busy thread runs for 25 ms, then sits parked for 75 ms. Average utilisation is 25%, but the shape is a 25 ms burst followed by a 75 ms stall. If that thread is serving requests, p99 latency now includes the stall.

I ran exactly this on a 3-vCPU Debian 13 host (kernel 6.12, systemd 257):

systemd-run --user --unit=cpu-lab --property=CPUQuota=25% \
  /bin/bash -c 'while :; do :; done'

systemctl --user show cpu-lab -p CPUQuotaPerSecUSec -p ControlGroup
# CPUQuotaPerSecUSec=250ms
# ControlGroup=/user.slice/user-1000.slice/user@1000.service/app.slice/cpu-lab.service

The kernel file matched the arithmetic:

$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/user.slice/user-1000.slice/user@1000.service/app.slice/cpu-lab.service/cpu.max
25000 100000

Sampling CPUUsageNSec over a 4.02 s window showed 1.005 s of CPU time consumed, or 25.0% of one CPU. Meanwhile cpu.stat showed the group had been throttled in 30 of 31 periods. It was not running slowly. It was running fast, then not at all.

That distinction drives most of the practical advice:

  • Latency-sensitive services usually want a generous quota plus a weight, not a tight quota. A tight quota converts load into tail latency.
  • Batch work that must not disturb anything else is the opposite case: a tight quota is correct, and stalls do not matter.
  • If you need finer-grained enforcement, shorten the period. Below ~10 ms you pay more accounting overhead for little gain, and systemd will not go below 1 ms.

Read the counters before changing anything

cpu.stat is where the truth is:

$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../cpu-lab.service/cpu.stat
usage_usec 792598
user_usec 781696
system_usec 10901
nr_periods 31
nr_throttled 30
throttled_usec 2247452
nr_bursts 0
burst_usec 0

The first three counters always exist. nr_periods, nr_throttled, throttled_usec, nr_bursts, and burst_usec appear when the controller is enabled, and only account for fair-class scheduling.

Two warnings about interpretation:

  • These five counters are not hierarchical. They report throttling caused by this cgroup's own limit, not throttling inherited from a parent slice. For the time actually lost including ancestors, read cpu.stat.local.
  • For a fully CPU-bound group, nr_throttled roughly equals nr_periods. That is normal, not a bug: the group always uses its whole budget and always hits the wall. A ratio near zero means the quota is not binding and the limit is decoration.

A useful rule of thumb: if throttled_usec divided by wall-clock time is above roughly 20%, the quota is shaping your workload's behaviour in a way users will feel.

Burst: borrow against future quiet time

cpu.max.burst (kernel file) lets a cgroup accumulate unused quota and spend it later, up to the value you set. Default is 0; the valid range is 0 to the current $MAX. nr_bursts and burst_usec in cpu.stat count the periods where it happened.

The kernel documentation describes this as borrowing against future underrun, and it is explicitly a trade: you keep the average, accept short interference with other groups, and stop throttling on spikes that are followed by idle time. It is a good fit for request-driven services with bursty CPU and a bad fit for a hard isolation requirement.

Not every kernel exposes the file. Check with ls in the cgroup directory before you plan around it.

cpu.weight is fairness, not a cap

cpu.weight lives in the range 1 to 10000, default 100. It only distributes CPU time among siblings that have runnable tasks. A lone service with weight 100 on an idle box still gets every core. Weight changes nothing until there is contention, and then it changes everything about who waits.

The split is proportional to weight among the children of the same parent. It is not transitive: two services inside system.slice compete with each other, but their weights do not let them outrank a unit in user.slice; the slice weights decide that level.

I measured a 100 vs 300 pair on 3 vCPUs, each unit running four busy threads so both would genuinely contend:

for w in 100 300; do
  systemd-run --user --unit="demo-$w" --property=CPUWeight=$w \
    /bin/bash -c 'for i in 1 2 3 4; do while :; do :; done & done; wait'
done

Two more details matter in production:

  • cpu.weight.nice is an alternative view using the familiar −20..19 range. It is a coarser mapping onto the same weight.
  • CPUWeight=idle sets cpu.idle, which makes the cgroup run only when nothing else in the same parent or its siblings wants the CPU. This is the right setting for backup indexers, thumbnailers, and anything that should consume leftovers.

cpuset: placement, partitions, and a delegation trap

cpuset.cpus restricts which CPUs a group's tasks may run on. systemd exposes it as AllowedCPUs= (since v244). The requested set is not the granted set: the effective set is the intersection with every ancestor, readable as EffectiveCPUs= in systemd and cpuset.cpus.effective in the kernel.

AllowedCPUs=2-5

On a 3-vCPU host, I tried AllowedCPUs=0 on a user unit and got EffectiveCPUs= empty with no cpuset.cpus file at all. The per-user manager on that host had only cpu memory pids in cgroup.controllers, so the cpuset controller was never available to apply the setting. The configuration was accepted and silently did nothing.

That is the trap: always verify placement with EffectiveCPUs, and run cpuset experiments as system units (or inside a delegated container cgroup) where the controller exists.

Beyond simple pinning, cgroup v2 supports cpuset partitions. Writing root to cpuset.cpus.partition turns a cgroup into a scheduling domain with exclusive CPUs from cpuset.cpus.exclusive. Writing isolated also removes scheduler load balancing and keeps unbound workqueues off those CPUs. Partitions can end up in an invalid state if the exclusive set overlaps a sibling's, and the file then reads back something like root invalid () — which is your cue to fix the hierarchy rather than the workload.

Use this when you genuinely want dedicated cores: latency-critical inference, DPDK-style packet processing, real-time-ish audio. Do not use it to "reserve" capacity you are not actually using; an isolated core with no runnable task is just an idle core nobody else may borrow.

cpuset.mems is the NUMA half of the same controller. On multi-socket boxes, pinning CPUs without pinning memory can send every access across the interconnect.

Wiring it into a unit, then proving it

A drop-in keeps the distribution unit file untouched:

# /etc/systemd/system/ffmpeg-worker.service.d/20-cpu.conf
[Service]
CPUAccounting=yes
CPUQuota=200%
CPUQuotaPeriodSec=100ms
CPUWeight=200
AllowedCPUs=0-1

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart ffmpeg-worker.service

For experiments you do not want to keep:

sudo systemctl set-property --runtime ffmpeg-worker.service CPUQuota=150%
# drop --runtime to persist the change as a drop-in

Verify the effective configuration rather than the file you wrote:

systemctl show ffmpeg-worker.service \
  -p CPUQuotaPerSecUSec -p CPUWeight -p AllowedCPUs \
  -p EffectiveCPUs -p CPUUsageNSec

CPUQuotaPerSecUSec=1.5s means 150% of one CPU. Empty EffectiveCPUs means your cpuset request is not being applied. And a live view of who is actually consuming:

systemd-cgtop -b -c -1 --depth=4

Note the flags: -b is batch mode, -c orders by CPU, -1 runs a single iteration. (-m orders by memory, which is a different thing.)

A reproducible lab

This script reports a unit's achieved CPU usage as a percentage of one CPU. It uses systemctl by default; set SYSTEMCTL="systemctl --user" to sample user units.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# cpu-usage.sh  [seconds]
set -euo pipefail
unit="${1:?usage: cpu-usage.sh  [seconds]}"
secs="${2:-10}"
sctl="${SYSTEMCTL:-systemctl}"

a=$($sctl show "$unit" -p CPUUsageNSec --value)
t0=$(date +%s%N)
sleep "$secs"
b=$($sctl show "$unit" -p CPUUsageNSec --value)
t1=$(date +%s%N)

awk -v a="$a" -v b="$b" -v e="$((t1 - t0))" -v u="$unit" 'BEGIN {
  printf "%s: %.1f%% of one CPU over %.2fs\n", u, (b - a) / e * 100, e / 1e9
}'

Full quota test:

  /bin/bash -c 'while :; do :; done'
sleep 3
SYSTEMCTL="systemctl --user" ./cpu-usage.sh cpu-lab 10
systemctl --user stop cpu-lab

Expected: roughly 25%, with nr_throttled close to nr_periods. If you see 100%, the controller is not active or the quota did not land; check cpu.max directly.

Then change the quota live and watch the number follow:

systemctl --user set-property --runtime cpu-lab CPUQuota=75%

Failure modes worth checking first

  • A quota below one request's CPU cost. The request cannot finish inside its slice, gets throttled, and latency explodes. Raise the quota, shorten the period, or accept that the service needs a weight instead.
  • "50% of the machine" thinking. CPUQuota=50% is half of one CPU, total, across all threads. On a 32-core host that is 1.5% of capacity.
  • Weights on an idle box. Nothing happens, correctly. Weight is a contention policy.
  • Weights across slices. A service cannot outrank a sibling slice by weight alone; the parent slice's weight sets the ceiling.
  • cpuset without the controller. AllowedCPUs= is accepted, EffectiveCPUs stays empty, and the service runs everywhere. Check delegation.
  • Real-time threads. cgroup v2's CPU bandwidth control does not cover real-time tasks in the way you might assume; the kernel documentation carries an explicit warning about CONFIG_RT_GROUP_SCHED and RT processes in non-root cgroups.
  • Autogrouping. sched(7) describes automatic session-based group scheduling, which behaves similarly to weights but is a different mechanism. Do not debug one while looking at the other.
  • Container runtimes writing the same file. A Kubernetes CPU limit and a systemd drop-in both end up in cpu.max. The last writer wins. When numbers disagree, cat the file.
  • Steal time on VMs. Quota is enforced against vCPU time. A guest can be far below its quota and still slow because the hypervisor is not scheduling it.

Rollback 

sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/ffmpeg-worker.service.d/20-cpu.conf
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart ffmpeg-worker.service
# or, to drop all local overrides for the unit:
sudo systemctl revert ffmpeg-worker.service

An empty CPUQuota= unsets the quota; cpu.max returns to max 100000. CPUWeight= unset returns the kernel default of 100.

CPU control is one of the few places where the kernel's model is simpler than the folklore. A quota is a per-period budget that ends in a hard stop. A weight is a tie-breaker that only matters when someone else wants the same cycles. A cpuset is placement. Pick the one that matches the promise you are making, then read cpu.stat and EffectiveCPUs to confirm the promise is being kept.

  • systemd.resource-control(5), CPUWeight=, CPUQuota=, CPUQuotaPeriodSec=, AllowedCPUs=: https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.resource-control.html
  • systemd-cgtop(1): https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd-cgtop.html
  • sched(7), autogroup feature: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/sched.7.html
  • Pressure stall information, cpu.pressure: https://docs.kernel.org/accounting/psi.html

  • cpuset without the controller. AllowedCPUs= is accepted, EffectiveCPUs stays empty, and the service runs everywhere. Check delegation.
  • Real-time threads. cgroup v2's CPU bandwidth control does not cover real-time tasks in the way you might assume; the kernel documentation carries an explicit warning about CONFIG_RT_GROUP_SCHED and RT processes in non-root cgroups.
  • Autogrouping. sched(7) describes automatic session-based group scheduling, which behaves similarly to weights but is a different mechanism. Do not debug one while looking at the other.
  • Container runtimes writing the same file. A Kubernetes CPU limit and a systemd drop-in both end up in cpu.max. The last writer wins. When numbers disagree, cat the file.
  • Steal time on VMs. Quota is enforced against vCPU time. A guest can be far below its quota and still slow because the hypervisor is not scheduling it.

Rollback 

sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/ffmpeg-worker.service.d/20-cpu.conf
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart ffmpeg-worker.service
# or, to drop all local overrides for the unit:
sudo systemctl revert ffmpeg-worker.service

An empty CPUQuota= unsets the quota; cpu.max returns to max 100000. CPUWeight= unset returns the kernel default of 100.

CPU control is one of the few places where the kernel's model is simpler than the folklore. A quota is a per-period budget that ends in a hard stop. A weight is a tie-breaker that only matters when someone else wants the same cycles. A cpuset is placement. Pick the one that matches the promise you are making, then read cpu.stat and EffectiveCPUs to confirm the promise is being kept.

Sources

  • Linux kernel documentation, Control Group v2, CPU and Cpuset controller sections: https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html
  • Linux kernel documentation, CFS Bandwidth Control: https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-bwc.html
  • systemd.resource-control(5), CPUWeight=, CPUQuota=, CPUQuotaPeriodSec=, AllowedCPUs=: https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.resource-control.html
  • systemd-cgtop(1): https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd-cgtop.html
  • sched(7), autogroup feature: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/sched.7.html
  • Pressure stall information, cpu.pressure: https://docs.kernel.org/accounting/psi.html

title: Censys Found 1,465 Exposed Artex AI-Attack Consoles. A Page Title Gave Them Away
summary:
• Book: Observability for LLM Applications
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

The AI agent framework behind two of October's intrusion campaigns runs a web console, and a lot of those consoles are sitting on the open internet. On November 5, Censys published the count: "As of November 4, 2026, Censys observed 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console."

These posts have followed Artex since WorkOS said it was likely behind an intrusion into its sales tool. The Censys post adds a census of where the consoles run and what runs beside them, plus the model traffic they leave behind. That last part you can check in your own logs today.

What Censys counted

Artex is an open-source, LLM-driven autonomous penetration testing framework, released on GitHub in July 2026. Microsoft describes it as "a system of LLM-driven agents that run an autonomous penetration test from reconnaissance through data exfiltration," and on October 21 tied it to a ConnectWise supply-chain compromise by a group it tracks as Storm-0940. Censys notes that CrowdStrike and Microsoft attributed malicious use to two separate campaigns that month.

The 1,465 hosts are not 1,465 operators. Censys says "about 650 sit in two blocks of identically configured hosting, which leaves roughly 815 distinct-looking deployments." TechCrunch reports those as more than 800 distinct deployments reachable from the web without a password.

By country, Censys lists 726 hosts in the United States, 387 in Hong Kong and 177 in China. It also says "some of the hosts publicly exposed are likely operated by authorized testers," so an exposed console is not proof of a crime. And it adds that "the ARTEX console does not require public-facing access, and overall global deployment is likely higher."

What sat next to the consoles

About one in ten consoles had company. According to Censys, 155 of the 1,465 Artex hosts (10.6%) also ran at least one other threat that Censys detects, led by CyberStrikeAI on 70 hosts, plus Vshell, Cobalt Strike and Adaptix C2.

Some operators also left files out. Censys counted 32 open directories on other Artex hosts at the time of writing, holding post-exploitation kits, stagers and implants. In the case CrowdStrike investigated, "the actor left open directories exposing a .claude folder, prompts, session histories, and ARTEX configuration files." Censys also describes one exposed home directory with .ssh and .bash_history in it, and another host exposing a MITM root CA private key.


Censys found the consoles the way any scanner finds a web app: by what the page says about itself.

A page title gave them away

The fingerprint is ordinary. Censys matched hosts whose HTML page title starts with "ARTEX" followed by a space, colon or dash, and whose page body references Next.js static assets under _next/static. The title half of its query reads:

web.endpoints.http.html_title=~"^ARTEX[ :—]"

The default console port is 8787/tcp, "with 8790 and 443 common," per Censys, which counted 1,931 endpoints on 8787 alone. It also sees customized builds, such as "ARTEX MX" on four adjacent hosts, plus a handful of other renamed consoles. A console whose title no longer starts with "ARTEX" falls outside this query.

None of that is specific to attack tooling. A self-hosted agent dashboard, an eval viewer or a prompt playground on a dev box announces itself the same way, through its title and its framework's asset paths. If it listens on every interface and the host has a public IP, a scanner can index it. Two standard commands show which address each listening port is bound to (lsof on macOS and Linux, ss on Linux):

# macOS or Linux: every listening TCP socket
lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN

# Linux: same, with the owning process
ss -ltnp

A local address of 127.0.0.1 or ::1 means loopback only. *, 0.0.0.0 or [::] means every interface, and that is the one to look at twice before you leave the machine running.

Check your egress logs for LLM proxies

The detail most relevant to anyone who ships LLM features is about model traffic. "43 ARTEX hosts also run self-hosted LLM gateway or reseller software, mainly CLIProxyAPI (19) and New API (18)," Censys writes. It says the actor in the CrowdStrike case used DeepSeek as the main model, likely bought through an API reseller, and ran Claude Code sessions backed by GLM and Grok. It also says Artex supports Anthropic, OpenAI and OpenAI-compatible endpoints.


The Censys advice for defenders is about the side pipe: model traffic going somewhere you didn't pick.

Its recommendation is one line: "For defenders, unfamiliar LLM proxies and resellers in egress logs are worth investigating." That only works if you know which model endpoints your own services are supposed to call. If every LLM call in your stack goes through one client or gateway that logs the base URL, a request to a reseller domain nobody chose stands out on the first query. If calls are scattered across services with their own SDK config, it is much harder to spot.

The rest of the hunting list from Censys, for teams that run detection:

  1. Search for the title fingerprint on 8787/tcp, then 8790 and 443.
  2. Check flagged hosts for co-located open directories, Vshell or FRP listeners, and LLM proxy software such as CLIProxyAPI or New API.
  3. Review scan history for mitmproxy banners and short-lived Python SimpleHTTP servers on high ports, which Censys says often appear before the console.
  4. Block or monitor the indicators it publishes, including the CrowdStrike and Microsoft IPs and the xcai[.]pro domain.

Closed source won't make it go away

The Artex author later stated the project would go closed-source with no further releases, and the repository has since been taken down, according to Censys. The same post says archived copies and rebrands are still circulating, and TechCrunch reports dozens of copies remain on code-sharing sites. TechCrunch also notes that many of the linked attacks got in through weak or known passwords and missing multi-factor authentication.

Rebrands will drift off the title fingerprint. The model calls still have to leave the network, so the egress log keeps showing them.

Do you know today which LLM endpoints your production services call, or would a reseller domain in your egress logs go unnoticed? Tell me in the comments.

If this was useful

The Censys advice comes down to one question: can you see where your model traffic goes? Observability for LLM Applications is my book on answering that for LLM features in production, from tracing every call to tracking cost and catching quality regressions. If the egress section above made you realize you couldn't list your own LLM endpoints, that's the visibility it helps you build.

I also build Hermes IDE, so weigh this mention with that in mind. It's a free, source-available desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux that runs Claude Code, Codex and other coding agents side by side, each in its own terminal, and each task can get its own worktree. It's on GitHub, and it isn't affiliated with Nous Research, Anthropic, OpenAI or any agent vendor.
